title: Part 7
text: the flood that tried to claim him came pouring back out in fits and stutters. He stayed down, forehead nearly in the mud, and let it happen, because there was nothing else to do and his body wasn't accepting other suggestions right now anyway. His limbs trembled with every retch — the ache in his leg flared white-hot as it twisted beneath him, a spike of pain so sharp it nearly reset his vision — but there was no room in his mind to process it yet. The world was loud and bright and spinning at the edges. He was barely aware of the yard around him — the debris, the receding water, the shapes of other people in various states of ruin nearby. He vaguely remembered darkness, pain. Could feel the echo of something that had been gripped tight in his hand. Something sharp against him. Why was his leg burning so much? All he could register was air — precious, stinging air — and the desperate pull of his lungs trying to rinse the wet out of his bloodstream one gasp at a time. Breathe first. Everything else later. Dwight slammed into the base of a twisted fence post, scrabbled against it to pull himself sitting upright out of the range of the tsunami that had carried him. The metal was cold and bent and the most solid thing he'd touched in hours and he was not letting go of it. He clung there, wide-eyed, coughing up dark water in wracking heaves while his body sorted itself out and his brain tried to catch up with the fact that there was sky above him. Actual sky. Not ceiling. Not water. Sky, and air, and the distant amber glow of streetlamps filtering through the trees at the yard's edge. A rogue corkboard clipped his leg on its way past, the last of the flood pulling it out in the nearby street to settle in the grass of a ditch. His breath hitched sharp, throat burning, eyes wide and stinging as he gagged up another mouthful of dark water that should not have been in his lungs. Relief hit jagged — messy and out of order — colliding with the taste of rust and panic still thick on his tongue. His chest convulsed again, wracked by coughs he couldn’t stop, but he wasn’t under anymore. He was here. He was out. And it was blindingly bright. Even at this hour, even through watering eyes, the outside world hit him like a physical thing after hours of the flashlight and the dark. He squinted hard against it and it didn't help and he didn't care, because bright meant outside and outside meant out. Something had hit him in the face on the way through. He couldn't place exactly when — somewhere between the wall coming apart and the fence post, a desk or a cabinet corner catching him across the cheekbone and peeling his glasses off. He could feel the throb of it already, the hot pressure of a bruise developing under his eye. Everything past a few inches was just colors and light and smeared shapes, adding to the blooming headache that promised to make the nausea worse down the line. All of it felt like the best thing that had ever happened to him. He pressed his forehead against the fence post and breathed. Orela hit the ground flat on her back in the mud, the impact knocking what little air she had left straight out of her lungs. She registered this slowly, in pieces — the sky above her, the cold wet ground beneath her, the violent convulsions that wracked her torso, dragging up more of the foul water in thick, painful coughs that rattled through her ribs like an aftershock. She blinked against the outside air, trying to get the world to resolve into something with edges, and mostly failed. Something had weight on her arm. She turned her head between spasms, following the pull, and found her own fist. Still closed, fingers locked tight around a handful of dark fabric. Danny's sleeve. She'd been holding it since the hallway, through the alcove, through the wall coming apart, through the yard — she'd held on through all of it without registering that she was doing it, and her hand apparently hadn't gotten the message that they were out. She looked past her fist to where the sleeve led. He was on his side facing her, close, unresponsive. Still. Water ran off him in thin streams into the mud. Cuts wept sluggishly at his hairline, his jaw, the raw patches along his forearms. A bruise had started forming along his jawline, dark and spreading. In the open air and the amber glow of the streetlamps, without the water and the dark to obscure it, he looked like something that had been through a great deal more than one bad trial. His chest was moving. Just barely — a stuttered, shallow rhythm, that couldn’t be nearly enough. Bit still. Stuttering. Present. She released a breath she hadn't known she was holding. Orela rolled toward him. It took more than it should have — her arms shaking under her weight, the mud uncooperative, her chest still heaving between coughs that had no interest in waiting their turn. She got up onto one elbow and reached for his wrist, probing for that extra reassurance that she didn’t actually — He jolted beneath her touch, limbs twitching sharp and uncoordinated. The movement was sharp and total, his whole body jerking away from the contact, eyes snapping open — wide, glassy, the whites catching the amber of the streetlamps. He tried to inhale and it caught somewhere in the middle, the breath seizing partway in, his hands scrabbling at the mud as he tried and failed repeatedly to push himself up. “Hey—” she rasped, voice shredded and soaked, palm flattening firm against his sternum, trying to push him back down, grounding him with what little steadiness she had left. “You’re ok. Breathe.” His eyes tracked. Slowly. Found her face. The breath came in on the second try — ragged, effortful, dragging through him with an audible wheeze that she was going to think about later in her nightmares. His body trembled as it rebooted — spine arching slightly, hands twitching where they’d curled toward his chest. He rolled fully onto his back with a pained sound and stared up at the sky, lips parted, trying to remember what lungs were supposed to do. His limbs hurt terribly, his chest felt bruised from the inside. She stayed propped on her elbow beside him, watching his chest move, and felt something in her unclench that had been wound tight since she found her teammates washed up in the hall outside of the basement. He couldn’t form words yet. Might not for a while. His face was slack with fatigue, still trapped somewhere between fight and shutdown. But he was alive. He natural rules of the trial domains that kept the survivors running through hell were working out here. He would recover. They all would. And Orela — coughs still tearing through her lungs, dirt caked to her face, every limb screaming — laughed. She’d gotten him out. Behind them, the school looked... small. Not dramatically — it hadn't collapsed, hadn't crumbled, hadn't done anything as overt as announcing that it was finished. It had simply stopped. The Entity, spent and denied, had withdrawn Her influence, and without Her the building had exhaled back into itself — the swollen doorframes shrinking to ordinary gaps, the bloated wood settling, the geometry quietly returning to something that matched its original footprint. The rotten blockades were gone as if they'd never been there. The hallways that had doubled and tripled in the dark were just hallways again. The lights inside flickered gently, soft yellow through cracked panes. If it weren't for the playground, you might not have known. The yard told the story the building no longer would — mud churned deep by the flood, dark puddles catching the amber of the streetlamps, debris scattered across the asphalt. Planks and plaster. A locker half-buried in the fence. The ghost of a hopscotch grid somewhere under all of it, invisible now, possibly permanent. And six people. Sprawled and propped and collapsed in various arrangements across the mud — waterlogged, bleeding lightly from a collection of minor and not-so-minor insults, flinching from the streetlamp glow that had no business being this bright after hours of nothing. Broken. Shaking. Alive. All of them. Ch 12 – Remnant Someone found a medkit in a locked chest near the fence line. Nobody questioned it — the Fog providing in the particular way it sometimes did, not generously exactly, but adequately. Orela took charge of it, grateful for something she could actually do something about, and went through the group in order of need. Jake's leg first — the cut from the Entity's claw cleaned and wrapped properly, the makeshift bandana job finally retired. Dwight's collection of minor insults next, the desk-shaped bruise under his eye, the scrapes from the fence post, the general catalogue of having been bounced off several things at speed. Orela even found his glasses in a bush a short way from the fence, one lens cracked but both still in the frame, and watched something visibly settle in him when she put them back in his hands. David and Jake were still coughing. The wet, rattling kind that didn't shift, that sat deep and announced its intentions to stay for a while. The others hovered, which David tolerated with approximately the same grace he tolerated everything tonight — jaw set, waving hands away, accepting help only when it was faster than arguing about it. Somehow, he was still upright, though even he wasn’t sure how. Getting back to camp would likely see him sleep for days. Leon came back around slowly, blinking against the streetlamp glow and fighting back random waves of nausea when the world refused to settle. A few tries to get upright. A brief, undignified introduction to what dizziness felt like when it really committed. He sat with his back against the fence and let the world sort itself out, head against his knees and shaking hands hidden away against his torso. David slipped away from the group while Orela was occupied with Leon. He didn't go far — just far enough to breathe without someone checking on him, rolling his shoulder and cataloguing the damage. The wet rattle of his lungs had settled in for the long haul, and every time he thought it was clearing it came back with interest. He'd deal with it. Nothing lasts in the Fog anyways. Off to the farthest end of the yard, he could see Danny trying very purposely to keep to himself. The man had found a section of fence to lean against, away from the group, and was attempting to wrap his own ribs with a strip of some random strip of fabric he sourced for who knows where. The attempt was not going well. His hands were clumsy with it, the fabric not cooperating, and every time he tried to pull it tight, he flinched and lost his grip and had to start over. It was obvious that he either had never done it before, or more likely had been in the Fog for so long that he had forgotten how to tend injuries. Being untouchable for years on end would have that effect, David mused, watching him struggle with the task. It’d be funny if it wasn’t so pathetic. Something soft bounced off the side of Danny’s head, making him startle slightly. He mentally cursed himself for the reaction, nerves entirely wound too tight. Unlike this damned fabric. Stupid shit kept coming loose when he tried to tie it. Glancing down to see what hit him, his hands paused their work. Laying in the grass was a small roll of bandages. He knew what those rolls did — had seen them work from the other side of a trial more times than he could count, watched survivors patch hook wounds and blade cuts in the middle of a chase and come back functional in minutes. The Fog's particular generosity with medical supplies had always struck him as one of its stranger qualities, that it would hand out tools that undermined the whole point of his job. But the point of the trial as a whole was fear, not damage, and fear didn't require permanent injury. He'd just never had occasion to use one himself. He picked it up. Looked across the yard. David met his eye for a hard moment before turning to go back to the others, busying himself with getting everyone stable and upright, swatting Orela away for the 20 th time in as many minutes. Danny looked at the bandage roll in his hand for a moment longer. Something complicated and uncomfortable settled into his chest, formless and unresolved, sitting alongside everything else the night had deposited there that he hadn't sorted through yet. He didn't have a name for it. Didn't particularly want to find one right now. He unwrapped the bandage and got to work. The difference was immediate — proper materials doing the job properly, the ache in his ribs dropping from a shout to a manageable complaint. He'd be sore for a while. But leagues better than before. The medkit died out too soon, as it always tended to do, but it was enough to get people functional. Walking-wounded functional, coughing-through-it functional, the usual grade of operational that the Fog seemed designed to maintain regardless of what the trial threw at people. It was always a little insane how well those kits worked. Tonight it felt more insane than usual. Nobody said it out loud — nobody had to. The trial didn't care what they'd been through. The gate wasn't opening without the work done, the campfire wasn't reachable without the gate, and standing in a flooded playground indefinitely wasn't an option anyone was willing to consider. So they went, in ones and twos, moving slower than usual but moving nonetheless, and finished what the night had interrupted. The last generator caught with a familiar surge, and the group moved together in an exhausted slog toward the gate as it ground open with the same shriek of rust and neglect it always made. The Fog met them at the threshold, and the first tendrils of it were an absolute blessing. The ache in bruised bones softening at the edges. The rawness in waterlogged lungs dulling toward something that might eventually become ordinary tired. The sharpest edges of the last several hours filing themselves down into something the mind could carry without bleeding. Danny trailed behind the group as they supported each other out of Bedham and towards the promise of a proper rest. Nobody had made a call for or against it. The logic had resolved itself somewhere in the yard while they were finishing the generators — he'd been there, he had nowhere else to be, and the group had collectively filed that under a problem for later and kept moving. He trailed a few feet behind David, water still dripping from his hair onto the gateway floor, and tried not to think too hard about what came next. The Entity’s barricades slammed up through the gate floor like knives, black and jagged, cleaving the path clean in half between Danny and the others. They howled as they emerged, shrieking metal and bone, driving a wedge between survivors and their tag-along. Everyone halted and turned back, the Fog briefly catching the shape of their surprise, as if the building and the water and the whole terrible night had temporarily made them forget what he was. Danny didn’t seem surprised. The gate had never been his. That was just the shape of things. It had always been a survivor’s exit — a path out of the trial and back to the fire. The best a killer could hope for, if they crossed it at all, was a return to their personal domain. And Danny didn't have one. He'd come into the Fog without a home — that was just the fact of it. No domain waiting for him, no personal architecture to return to between trials. He'd made do. He drifted. Crashed with others. Slept in corners of Myers’ neighborhood when no one noticed. Used houses that had long since lost their original owners. It was a comfortable life, floating untethered from domain to domain, as if the entirety of the Entity’s realm itself had been his home. He'd never been to their campfire. None of his kind had. That door had never been open to him and he hadn't expected it to be. Danny met David’s gaze through the barricade, gave a tight nod he hoped was reassuring, and motioned for him to go on without him. He stood on his side of the barricade and looked at Danny through the gaps in the spikes with that same unreadable expression from across the yard. For a moment he looked almost like he might come back to the barrier, eyes glancing over the spikes as if there was something to be done about them, before the tension dropped from his shoulders and he sighed lightly. He gave a single nod. Small. The particular weight of it landing somewhere between acknowledgement and something Danny didn't have a clean name for. Then he turned and rejoined the group, and the Fog took them, and the gateway sat empty with its spikes still up. Danny stood at the barrier for a while. The Fog beyond it showed him nothing — just the soft grey of a domain's edge, the suggestion of a path he wasn't going to take. He watched the space where the group had been until his sides started to ache lightly again, the headache he had jolted back to awareness with threatening to return around the edges of his vision. Nothing more he could do here anyways. So, he turned back into the domain. The street was quiet in the perpetual night of the domain — the generators finished, the gate opened, the survivors gone and the trial technically over. Whatever the Fog did with itself in the spaces between, it did it silently. Usually, he would have been spirited away by now and dumped into the next area. Being able to freely wander an empty domain after a trial felt wrong somehow. Danny wandered the empty street, each step squelching softly through mud and silt, until the familiar bulk of the preschool rose into view again. The surrounding area had taken the full force of the exit — the yard churned, the fence buckled in places where lockers had introduced themselves to it, plaster and debris scattered across the asphalt and pooling in the gutters. The building itself looked scoured. Pressure washed empty, and left to drip dry across the lawn. It wasn't permanent. He knew that. The next time a trial was called here the Fog would reset the whole domain — pull the debris back, drain the water, restore the geometry to its original footprint and set the crows back on their perches as if none of it had happened. That was just how it worked. The Fog didn't hold onto damage. He wasn't sure yet if that was a comfort. The absence was what hit hardest. The rot, the weight, the invisible pulse of malice that had choked the walls for hours — it was gone. No pressure at the edges of his awareness. No sense of being observed. Just the domain, and the debris, and the distant sound of water still draining somewhere in the building's bones. She had spent Herself on this. Used everything She had and come away empty-handed, and now She was simply — gone. Recovering somewhere in the architecture of Her own realm, presumably. Licking Her wounds. He limped through the yard, sidestepping a half-sunk filing cabinet in the mud. His ribs reminded him of their existence with every step — the bandage was doing its work, but it’s not like it could perform miracles. The debris was everywhere — lockers wedged against the fence at improbable angles, plaster smeared in wide arcs across the rusted swing set, a filing cabinet embedded nose-first in a flower bed that had never had flowers in it. The playground wore the evidence of the night — it, too, seemed to be a victim of the Entity’s little game. He picked his way through it slowly, not in any particular hurry, the silence of it settling around him one step at a time. He reached the side entrance and kicked a chunk of door frame out of the path. Then another. The broken killer wall gaped open above the debris line, the edges of it ragged and splintered outward, wood shrapnel scattered across the grass in an impressive radius. Danny toed aside a chunk of molding, eyeing the wreckage with something almost like respect. The damage was impressive. Not just the final breach — the whole face of the wall told the story of what had happened in the alcove, the wood bearing the accumulated record of every kick in a pattern of stress fractures that radiated outward from the centre. Whatever the killer walls were made of, it wasn't meant to come apart like this. It wasn't meant to come apart at all. That was the point of them. Danny ran his fingers along the splintered edge, reading the force of it in the grain. “...Gold star, brawler,” he muttered with a slight chuckle. The stocky little brat had been underwater, out of air, running on something past exhaustion and past rage and past whatever came after rage — and he'd broken the damned wall anyway. Danny pulled his hand back from the wood. He turned the thought over once, quiet and private in the empty domain. If the man ever had the inclination to swap sides — the desire, the circumstance, whatever it would take — he would be a genuinely terrifying thing to face in a trial. The Fog would probably be delighted. The survivors considerably less so. Danny leaned against the doorframe and let it hold some of his weight. The ribs made themselves known about that, a low persistent complaint that the bandage was managing but not solving. He'd be dealing with them for a while. He was used to discomfort, generally speaking — the Fog had a particular relationship with pain that kept things functional without making them comfortable — but this was a specific, personal kind of ache that felt different from the usual wear of a trial. More earned, maybe. Definitely deserved, at the very least. He leaned against the splintered doorway, letting his shoulder slump against the frame. The hallway inside was back to normal. Tight. Short. Still cracked and peeling in that aesthetic decay way, but no longer a shapeshifting maze full of pressure and current. No longer a black chasm of currents and chaos. No screaming. He hadn't expected to feel anything in particular about that. Still, there was a strange sort of relief; the specific comfort of a space that was just a space again and wasn't trying to kill anyone. After the hallways stretching and the currents and the pipes and the ceiling arriving in increments, ordinary was something he could handle. Ordinary gave him the time to stop, rest a bit, and let the silence of it settle around him, trying not to think too hard about what came next. He pushed off from the doorframe. There was likely somewhere in the building that was probably drier than the rest of it. If not, there were other small, busted buildings in the area that would suffice. He could sleep off the ribs and the shaking and the general accumulated damage of the night, and then figure out the rest from there. That was enough of a plan for now. Turning to start up the hunt for a passable nap spot, something caught his eye. He stopped. Turned back slowly, not sure yet what he'd seen, just the peripheral awareness of something that didn't fit — a quality of light, a stillness that struck differently somehow. One of the classrooms off the main hallway. He looked at it for a moment from the corridor. A single desk sat in the middle of the floor. The rest of the room was the same wreckage as everywhere else — waterlogged, debris- strewn, the detritus of the night settling wherever gravity had put it. But the desk was clear. Centred. The streetlight came through the window at an angle that caught it directly, the amber glow pooling across the surface, making it look almost like an altar. He drifted forward, feet whispering through the remaining puddles that sat still and undisturbed on the tile. In the center of the desk sat his robe. Clean. Dry. The leather smooth and unmarked, the canvas underlayer pressed flat, the whole thing arranged with intent that bordered on domestic care. His mask rested on top, face up, the white of it catching the streetlight from the window. His phone and knife bordering it to either side. All of it exactly as it had been before the night started. His entire identity, returned to him like a present. A prize for surviving. Maybe a punishment for not dying. Danny stood in front of the desk and dripped quietly onto the floor. He looked at his things for a long moment without touching them, the clear message from them gently circling his mind. Time’s up. Get back to work. That was what this was. Not a gift — it had never been a gift; he understood that now with a clarity that the night had earned him the hard way. A summons. The gear cleaned and folded and waiting, because tools got maintained between uses, because that was what you did with something you intended to keep using. The cleaning wasn't kindness. It was just upkeep. He'd known, in the abstract, that this was how it worked. He'd always known. The killers weren't here because She loved them — they were here because She needed them, and need was a transactional thing. He'd told himself the autonomy he'd carved out was real, that the space between the trials was his, that the arrangement was something he'd chosen to participate in rather than something he'd been slotted into. The water in the schoolyard said otherwise. She had turned Her domain into a trap and put him in it with the survivors without warning or protection, and when it stopped serving Her purposes, She had simply — withdrawn. Left him to whatever came next. The gear on the desk was not an apology. It was a reminder of what he was for, laid out under a streetlight like a receipt. He knew better than to disobey. He had seen what Her displeasure looked like up close tonight, felt it in the current that had no interest in which side of the trial he was supposed to be on. If She decided he wasn't worth the trouble of maintaining, that was simply what would happen. They were all tools. Every one of them. Expected to be grateful She'd found a use for them at all. He picked up the robe. The leather was dry. Clean. Lighter than it had been in the hallway, obviously — waterlogged was a different animal entirely — but he suspected She had given back his strength before withdrawing as well. He stood with it in his hands for a moment, feeling the familiar weight of it. Eventually, with hands that trembled more than he wanted to admit, he dressed. Layer by layer, the same way it came off — in reverse, without ceremony, the buckles finding their positions with the muscle memory of a hundred trials. The cowl. The gloves. The whole assembled architecture of the thing, rebuilt around him in the amber light of an empty classroom while water dripped quietly in the hallway behind him. He picked up the knife last. Ran his thumb along the worn edge of the handle, the familiar curves of it sitting in his palm exactly as they always had. He waited for the thing that usually came with it — the sharpening of attention, the quiet pleasure of holding something he was good at using. The sense of himself clicking back into place. It didn't come. He closed his hand around the handle anyway and slid it home. He knew how the next trial would go. He'd stalk, and he'd slash, and he'd play the game the way he'd always played it, because that’s what was expected of him and he knew better than to refuse. He'd find the rhythm of it again eventually. Maybe even the fun. The Fog had a way of smoothing things over, filing the edges down, making the distances between things feel longer than they were. But for a select few, he would hold back. Not many. Just a handful. Just enough to make a difference that nobody would be able to measure or name — a fraction of a second's hesitation, a hook instead of a blade, a hatch left open for no particular reason. Not mercy. He wasn't prepared to call it that. Just a fraction. Just enough. The smallest seeds of doubt, buried deep in the Fog.
